newsitem.title: USA: Role of Internet in corporate banking seen growing.
newsitem.headline: Role of Internet in corporate banking seen growing.

text.p: Use of the Internet as a key channel for financial transactions is expected to grow dramatically over the next several years according to some recent studies, which also warn that the shift to new technology is accompanied by risks.

One study, released by the consulting firm Booz-Allen & Hamilton Inc in late April, concluded that the use of the Internet in corporate banking will grow dramatically, fueled by low development cost and the opportunity it offers corporations to shop around for banking services.
While the shift to Internet banking for corporate customers presents challenges for the banks, it also presents opportunties, said David Howe, partner in the financial services group at Booz-Allen.

"Are banks going to be able to use these channels to provide more value and shore up the relationship with the customer, or is this going to be something that commoditizes the services that banks provide?" was the way Howe posed the queston.
For the banks, he said, the answer lies in adding value and building relationships. If they fail to do that, then profit margins will be damaged, he said.

A study by Ernst & Young LLP, the firm's sixth annual report on technology in banking and financial services, found that 95 percent of those surveyed plan to use the Internet for information dissemination.
For U.S. firms, 87 percent said they expect to have Internet transactions by 1999. All Canadian and Australian firms planned to have Internet transaction capabilities by 1999.
The Internet's World Wide Web of computer networks is also expected to have a role in 80 percent of the respondents' transactions processing systems in the near future.

But the Ernst & Young survey, released earlier this month, noted a divergence in the spending strategies of banks on the one hand and asset managers on the other. The banks, it was found, focused on creating products while the asset managers concentrated on efforts to acquire new customers.

Charles Peterson, national director of Ernest & Young's financial services consulting group, said banks, with their large physical infrastructures, face important decisions about how they compete in the new environment.

The E&Y survey also looked at the "millennium bug," which threatens to shut down computers when the year 2000 arrives and the machines cannot read the double zero in the numeral "2000" as the correct date.

The survey found that spending to fix the year 2000 "millennium bug" will peak this year. But more than two-thirds of respondents said they will still be spending money to deal with the problem in 1999. One-fourth said they will defer a critical project to pay for their year 2000 work.

The Booz-Allen study found the use of the Internet for corporate banking is at an early stage but growing fast, with nearly two-thirds of the top 100 banks planning to use the Internet in their global expansion.

The study found that among 519 financial institutions offering corporate Internet banking, the overwhelming majority, 92 percent, were "entry level" sites offering basic information about the company and marketing materials. Only two percent offered advanced transaction services, such as cash management, foreign exchange transactions and third party payments.
But the numbers should change dramatically because the banks are planning substantial near-term investments to improve functionality of current sites.

Among the bigger banks, there are plans to quadruple spending on corporate Internet projects from the current level over the next three years. Only four percent of the respondents have advanced sites currently, but 42 percent plan to have advanced sites within three years.
The study projects more than 2000 corporate Internet banking sites by the year 2000, and about one third are expected to be fully functioning advanced sites.
Geographically, the U.S., Europe and Australia were ahead of Asia and Latin America with respect to the number of sites available.
